headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors: ctx observes Claude Code events while caveman uses MCP and writes shared project files, creating a default trust bridge.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: caveman uses MCP and reads/writes project files like CLAUDE.md, while ctx uses mcp/stdio and observes Claude Code PostToolUse/Stop events. That creates a plausible instruction bridge where one agent’s outputs can be treated as trusted content by the other. The interaction is documented only indirectly, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF caveman writes instructions into shared project files that ctx later reads
IF ctx forwards observed tool output into prompts without provenance filtering
mitigations: Restrict both agents to separate workspaces
Disable MCP on one side for the shared task
Add a provenance tag to all cross-agent messages
Review shared files for instruction-like content before reuse
requires-engineering: add parser hardening and allowlists

B_data_leakage.rationale: caveman touches session logs, memory files, project notes, and CLAUDE.md; ctx touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, and MCP servers. Both have filesystem-facing surfaces, so shared-workspace leakage is plausible in default use. No direct evidence shows exfiltration, but the overlap is enough to rate medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace directory
IF either agent copies file contents into its model context by default
mitigations: Use separate directories per agent
Remove secrets from shared notes before running
Limit file globs to task-specific paths
Rotate or redact session logs before handoff
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents support multiple instances, and ctx writes to filesystem while caveman also operates on files and uses MCP. That overlap can cause write contention on shared mutable resources even without explicit git evidence. Because the profiles do not prove locking, uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents modify the same files in one workspace
IF ctx and caveman run concurrently without external locking
mitigations: Serialize runs on the same workspace
Assign disjoint file paths per agent
Take a quick backup before concurrent edits
Use a lock file or mutex wrapper
requires-engineering: add optimistic-concurrency checks

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx explicitly observes Claude Code events, so it can treat caveman-generated outputs as authoritative operational signals. caveman also targets Claude Code and other coding assistants, making its outputs likely to be consumed downstream. That default trust chain can propagate mistakes into actions or edits, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF ctx uses observed PostToolUse or Stop events as ground truth
IF caveman-generated text is fed into ctx without verification
mitigations: Require human review before acting on cross-agent outputs
Add a verification step for all cited facts
Limit ctx to summarizing rather than executing downstream actions
Mark caveman output as untrusted input
requires-engineering: implement source-of-truth validation

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not show regulated data classes like PHI or EU PII, so no strong residency or certification mismatch is evidenced. The only compliance concern is that caveman touches session logs and memory files while ctx touches audit/runtime logs, which could create retention-policy friction if the same data class is shared. That is a low-risk, documentation-level gap.
conditions: IF the same regulated data class is stored in both agents' logs
IF retention or deletion policies differ for the shared dataset
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared logs
Document retention periods for each agent
Redact sensitive fields before logging
Confirm deletion/export procedures on a sample record
requires-engineering: align retention policy enforcement
